rationale: Attachment can flatten benthic tests and Globigerina is typically trochospiral, but foraminiferal coiling geometry is phylogenetically and developmentally diverse rather than controlled by one planar force.
Foraminifera show substantial phenotypic plasticity, but modern species and genus distinctions generally reflect persistent morphological and genetic lineages rather than merely temporary variants.
Shell forms differ in ecological and reproductive performance, and their diversity and persistence do not imply equal fitness or an absence of selection.
A constrained shell-building process and limited morphospace make repeated convergent test forms plausible and well aligned with widespread homoplasy in microorganisms.
The recovery of delicate shells does not show that breakage is unimportant in life, and shell strength can affect predation, transport, dissolution, and survival.
Hydrodynamic sorting strongly affects where empty foraminiferal tests accumulate, although living distributions and shell abundance also depend on habitat, productivity, dissolution, and transport.
Physical constraints can generate convergent forms, so morphology alone is unsafe evidence of close kinship and phylogenetic classification must account for homoplasy.

Differential growth can curve a horn and bilateral placement limits gross lateral deviation, but an exact planar logarithmic spiral and constant growth-rate ratio are idealizations not established for rhinoceros horns generally.
Paired bovid horns are bilaterally homologous structures and normally exhibit opposite handedness as approximate mirror images, apart from individual asymmetry.
Many horns approximate spiral curves through differential growth, but exact logarithmic form and a constant opposite-side growth ratio across the great majority are overly restrictive.
These horns can be compared as progressively tighter approximate spirals, but the claimed homologous logarithmic series and precise constant angles are not robust general biological measurements.

Closely related wild sheep can share broad curvature while differing in torsion, but near-identical logarithmic angles and chiefly helical species differences are an oversimplified morphometric account.

The geometric model plausibly links opposed differential growth to planar curvature and offset extrema to torsion, but real horns have complex three-dimensional growth fields and the asserted usual cause is not established.
Mechanical interaction with the bony core may influence horn sheath shape, but evidence that unequal adhesion is often the chief generator of spiral curvature is weak relative to patterned growth.
Cross-sectional size can affect curvature mechanics, but horn thickness and spiral curvature vary independently across taxa and do not support this broad monotonic rule.

Torsion can distort surface markings, but attributing sinuous horn annuli specifically to elastic torsional strain with the predicted prism solution, and their absence in oxen, is insufficiently supported.
Circumnutation is produced by changing differential growth around elongating stem regions, although growth is concentrated in growth zones rather than occurring uniformly along the whole stem.

Frictional contact with a rough support can mechanically induce torsion, but stem twisting also reflects intrinsic growth and can have functional consequences, so the exclusive explanation is too strong.
Many antlers have a roughly planar or cupped branching pattern, but cervid antlers are diverse three-dimensional structures whose paired tines do not generally lie on one smooth spheroidal surface.
Continuous differential accretion commonly creates curved claws, beaks, and tusks, but it does not universally produce logarithmic spirals across all these structurally distinct organs.
Proboscidean tusks share accretionary growth and often curve, but species differ in cross-section, torsion, curvature, and growth trajectory, not merely final size along one logarithmic spiral.

Cylindrical and capitular phyllotaxis are geometric manifestations of sequential organ placement on differently shaped growing surfaces, though real transformations also involve changing growth and packing.

Regular initiation can generate ordered phyllotaxis, but similar timing and placement alone do not necessitate helices or logarithmic spirals without assumptions about divergence angle and surface growth.

Ideal logarithmic parastichies intersect at constant angles, but actual sunflower parastichies are developmental packing patterns and near-orthogonal visible families are not demonstrably an infrequent special case.
Conifer species often have characteristic low Fibonacci parastichy pairs, including approximately 3/5 in spruce and 5/8 in larch, although substantial within-species variation occurs.
Larger capitula accommodate more primordia and commonly express higher consecutive Fibonacci parastichy numbers, as observed among sunflower heads.
Phyllotactic chirality generally lacks a consistent population-level bias, and the stated spruce counts are close to the binomial expectation of equal handedness.
For an ideal single generative spiral, visible parastichy families are alternative neighbor connections in the same lattice, so a Fibonacci pair mathematically entails the lower-order connections.
The common golden-angle regime corresponds to roughly 2.6 organs per turn and generates Fibonacci parastichies, while other divergence regimes generate related series.
Organ proportions and packing determine which neighbor spirals look conspicuous, but divergence angle also determines the lattice and therefore cannot generally be declared irrelevant.
Golden-angle phyllotaxis has biological significance because developmental interaction and packing can favor efficient, nonrepeating placement; it is not merely a numerical coincidence.
Low-order distichous and common spiral arrangements are widespread across plants, whereas very high-order Fibonacci fractions generally require large, densely packed structures and are rarer.

Internode elongation strongly reduces vertical overlap, but divergence angle also materially affects light interception, especially in compact shoots, so it cannot be dismissed as an optimization mechanism.

Modern developmental models and comparative evidence support functional consequences and possible selection on phyllotactic packing, even though Fibonacci numbers arise indirectly rather than being selected as numbers.
Hard-shelled amniote eggs are overwhelmingly prolate or near-spherical rather than discoidal, but the universal 'never oblate' wording is vulnerable to exceptional shapes and deformation.

Oviductal mechanics contribute to egg shape before calcification, but membrane properties, isthmus geometry, developmental regulation, and evolutionary ecology also matter, making radial pressure an inadequate sole essential cause.
Relative egg size can affect constraints during formation, but broad comparative work links avian egg asymmetry to multiple factors, and the named taxa do not establish a common causal rule.
Pullet eggs are typically smaller and egg dimensions change with laying age, but a general shift from spherical first eggs to less spherical later eggs and the breed-level relation are variable.
Bird eggs commonly pass blunt end first and oviduct contractions shape the forming egg, but the asserted pressure maximum and direct production of the two ends are not a settled general mechanism.

This is the local Young-Laplace force balance for a pressurized membrane under the stated idealization, but nonuniform anisotropic membranes and solidifying shells prevent it from being a complete equation of all eggs.

Tension and failure location depend on local curvature, thickness, material anisotropy, and pressure; a universal maximum at the small end and concentration of abnormalities there are not well established.
Schistosoma mansoni is a valid, genetically and biologically distinct species, and its lateral-spined eggs are a stable diagnostic trait rather than a mere uterine variant of S. haematobium.
Echinoid test shape is built by patterned skeletal growth and plate architecture; gravity and tube-foot forces can deform flexible animals but do not generally mould tests as liquid drops.

Laplace scaling relates vessel radius, pressure, wall tension, and thickness, and distal pressures fall, but vascular composition and capillary one-cell walls make the proposed proportional sequence only qualitative.

Laplace-type wall-stress relations predict effects of curvature and the ventricular apex is relatively thin, but myocardial thickness is also governed by pressure, fiber architecture, loading, and active contraction rather than this exact formula.
Systemic ventricular pressure substantially exceeds pulmonary pressure, but normal left-ventricular wall thickness is not generally six to seven times the right, so the claimed matching ratio fails.

Vascular geometry exhibits energetic optimization consistent with Murray-type principles, but it balances pumping, blood volume, regulation, robustness, and development rather than simply minimizing wall area.
Optimal and observed bifurcations generally place a smaller daughter at a larger deflection and symmetric daughters symmetrically, though exact angles vary with anatomy and flow.
For a branch junction optimized with fixed endpoints and per-length energetic costs, vector balance yields a cosine relation of this kind, although biological vessels face additional constraints.
Mechanical performance can indeed be quantified, but camouflage, warning coloration, and mimicry are also experimentally demonstrable, so the asserted contrast is false.
Fresh cortical bone has tensile strength of the same order as, though usually below, its compressive strength, making it effective under both tension and compression.
Moving material away from the neutral axis gives hollow tubes high bending stiffness per mass, a principle clearly expressed in long bones, quills, and many plant stems.
Long-bone cortices are generally thickest in the diaphysis and thin toward the epiphyses, consistent with bending demands, although in-vivo bending moments are not a simple midspan curve.

Trabecular orientation correlates with principal loading directions and often forms crossing systems, but the classic claim of exact stress trajectories and right-angle correspondence is now regarded as approximate.
Trabeculae adapt through cell-mediated formation and resorption under mechanotransductive signals, not by shear physically displacing oblique struts into alignment.

Bone remodels its trabecular architecture in response to altered loading after fracture, but complete reorganization within weeks and the exclusion of inherited developmental control are overstatements.
Mechanical loading and strain are potent signals for tissue growth and remodeling, and compensatory bone hypertrophy is well established, though responses depend on strain regime and biology.
The quadruped trunk can be usefully analyzed as a beam supported by limbs, but its muscles and ligaments create bowstring and arch-like actions, so it is not strictly a double cantilever.
Many large quadrupeds carry a majority of static weight on the forelimbs, with horses near the stated range; the exact fractions vary by species, posture, and gait.
Neural spine height relates to ligament and muscle leverage under bending loads, but it is not simply proportional to local bending moment and serves multiple locomotor functions.

Regional spine enlargement often reflects leverage needed for heavy heads, tails, and locomotion, but the listed fossil and living patterns are influenced by musculature and posture and do not obey one universal load rule.

Buoyancy reduces weight-support demands and fully aquatic mammals show altered spines, but pinnipeds retain terrestrial loading and aquatic birds such as penguins can have robust specialized pelves, defeating the universal compound claim.

Fish vertebral processes can stiffen the trunk in several planes, but three ligament-connected series at near-exact 120-degree spacing and maximal uniform strength are not a general vertebrate pattern.
Vertebral columns do balance load-bearing strength against flexibility, but comparison with an engineer's cantilever and the claimed causal explanation of relative depth are qualitative.
Mechanical loading strongly shapes bone geometry and remodeling from trabeculae to whole skeletons, although development, ancestry, muscles, and cellular regulation also substantially determine form.
Convergent mechanics can mislead phylogeny, but individual bones often contain many heritable characters and can provide reliable evidence when analyzed comparatively rather than in isolation.
Changed loading commonly produces integrated, graded responses across correlated tissues, but evolutionary change can also be mosaic and localized rather than necessarily whole-body.

Both living and nonliving forms obey physics and deviate from ideals under multiple forces, but active growth, regulation, heredity, and feedback make organic form more than an ideal figure perturbed by secondary forces.
Closely related species often differ conspicuously in allometric proportions, but topology, counts, tissue specializations, and discrete developmental changes also cause specific differences.

Coordinate deformations can summarize some related shapes elegantly, but no general rule maps diverse organisms by one simple symmetric grid deformation or identifies a simple external force as its cause.
Correlated whole-body variation is real, but geometric mappings do not prove a comprehensive growth law and are fully compatible with natural selection acting on integrated developmental systems.
Tectonic strain commonly shears and flattens fossils in regular ways and has historically produced taxonomic misinterpretation, although 'often' depends on the fossil group and preservation.

Ruminant cannon bones show strong allometric elongation and the approximate width ratios are plausible, but saying relative length and breadth are their only essential differences overlooks shape and structural details.

Differential radial and tangential growth can mathematically transform ideal leaf outlines, but dicot leaf forms arise from spatial gene regulation, polarity, and localized growth rather than one universal ratio around a fixed basal node.
Differential growth across the midrib does produce Begonia leaf asymmetry, but the two sides are not generally exact similar figures related by a constant angular proportion.
